Assess safety of the patient and others and determine the need for hospitalization, intensive outpatient therapy, and/or close monitoring. A

First-line therapy is mood stabilizers such as lithium, valproate and lamotrigine. Antipsychotic agents (quetiapine, aripiprazole, asenapine, capiprazine, and lurasidone) may be effective but have significant adverse effects. A

background.definition: Bipolar disorder, previously known as manic-depressive disorder, is a mood disorder characterized by significant alternations in mood, energy, and functioning. Individuals experience periods of depression, (hypo)mania, mixed states, and asymptomatic periods of euthymia.

list.listitem: Adults: Data from the World Mental Health surveys from 2001-2022 across 29 countries reported a lifetime prevalence of bipolar disorder of 2.5% (95% CI, 2.4%-2.7%) in men and 2.3% (95% CI, 2.1%-2.4%) in women.
Children and adolescents: Lifetime prevalence in a community sample is 10/1000 person/years.
A study found that about 7% of primary care patients diagnosed with depression have unrecognized bipolar disorder, based on a study of 236 patients who took the Mood Disorder Questionnaire.
$38 billion lost productivity/year of patients and caregivers.
Bipolar disorder is caused by a complex combination of biologic, genetic, and environmental factors, which are still being investigated.
Twin, adoption, and epidemiological studies provide evidence for a strong genetic component to the etiology.
Although many genes and various abnormalities in the brain are associated with bipolar disorder, the exact mode of transmission is unknown.
The less than 100% concordance rate of monozygotic twins suggests that nongenetic factors, including stressful events, also contribute to the development and progression of the disorder.
Screen patients with symptoms of depression, irritability, or impulsivity for bipolar disorder using a validated instrument. C
Refer patients with suspected bipolar disorder to a psychiatrist for a comprehensive psychiatric interview. Earlier diagnosis and treatment are associated with a better prognosis. C
Assess safety of patient and others and determine need for hospitalization, intensive outpatient therapy, and/or close monitoring. C
Assess for any neurological conditions, medical conditions, medications, or substance abuse that may cause, contribute to, or complicate the disease process. C
Assess patients for common comorbid disorders, including substance, anxiety, eating, and personality disorders. About 7% initially diagnosed with depression meet criteria for bipolar disorder. B

Differential.Differential_Features: No history of manic, hypomanic, or mixed episodes; less often characterized by psychomotor retardation, atypical symptoms, and psychosis
Chronic rather than episodic, lack of clear onsets and offsets, no psychotic feature or abnormally expansive mood
Pervasive disorder of mood, thought, and behavior typically associated with marked decline in social functioning; periods of psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood symptoms
Fear or worry, no psychotic symptoms, no history of mania or hypomania
Pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, affect, and self-image

Differential.Differential_Name: Mood disorder due to a general medical condition
Differential.Differential_Features: Mood disturbance is a physiological consequence of a general medical condition
Mood disturbance is a physiological consequence of a substance
Period of psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood symptoms; periventricular white matter changes

list.listitem: See for DSM-V-TR criteria for mania, for hypomania, and for comparison between Bipolar I and II. See for criteria for bipolar depression.

Bipolar I can be distinguished from bipolar II disorder because it is associated with mania that causes significant impairment in occupational or social functioning; there may be psychotic features; hospitalization may be necessary to prevent harm to self or others. It can occur with or without a history of major depressive episodes.

Bipolar II disorder is not associated with mania and is characterized by at least one major depressive episodes and one hypomanic episode. The episode does not cause significant impairment; psychotic features do not occur during hypomania, and hospitalization is not required during mania; however, hospitalization may be required during depression.

Cyclothymia refers to a chronic mood disorder characterized by chronic, fluctuating mood swings that include peroids of hypomanic symptoms and peroids of depressive symptoms. They are not as severe as those defined for bipolar disorder diagnosis (symptoms last for at least two years in adults, one year in children and adolescents; and must occur for at least half the time without being absent for more than two consecutive months) .

An increasing number of patients are being diagnosed based on subthreshold criteria (i.e., not meeting formal criteria, specified as bipolar disorder NOS), increasing from 3.6% of diagnoses in 1999 to 73% in 2010.
Ask patient about family and personal history of mental/substance use disorders and responses to any previous treatment.

Ask about the use of medications and drugs that could cause symptoms of mania or depression (cocaine, PCP, amphetamines, anabolic steroids, caffeine, asthma medication for bronchodilation, antidepressants, and anti-Parkinson drugs).
Assess a patient's mental status with particular attention to suicidal/homicidal ideation, judgment, insight, mood, cognition, thought disorder, and anxiety.

Assess for comorbidity of other mental and medical disorders, psychosocial stressors, and patient's functional status. Approximately 65% of those with bipolar disorder have 1 or more concominant psychiatric disorders.
A study of 236 primary care patients diagnosed with depression but without known bipolar disorder found that about 7% met criteria for bipolar disorder.

Ask about adverse childhood events. Cross-sectional and longitudinal studies have shown increased prevalence of childhood maltreatment and its association with mood disorders, comorbidities, and suicidality.

Ask about homelessness. The prevalence of mental health disorders is higher in the homeless population than the general population. These patients will need individualized support and coordination in their management.
Routine laboratory testing or imaging is not required for all patients.

If hyperthyroidism is suspected, order thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). In patients with an abnormal neurological examination or worrisome signs of CNS disease, obtain an MRI. If symptoms could represent a seizure disorder, order EEG. If nutritional deficiency is suspected, order B12, folate, and thiamine. If substance abuse is suspected, order urine or blood toxicology.
Consider brain imaging and neurology consultation in atypical presentation of new-onset psychotic symptoms.

Before prescribing carbamazepine, order pregnancy test, CBC with differential and platelet count, liver function, thyroid function tests, and possibly serum sodium level. Consider ECG if history of cardiac arrhythmia.Serious and sometimes fatal dermatologic reactions, including toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, have been reported with carbamazepine. Patients with ancestry in genetically at-risk populations (broad area of Asia) should be screened for the presence of HLA-B*1502 prior to initiating treatment with carbamazepine.
Before prescribing valproate, order pregnancy test, CBC, liver and thyroid functioning tests.
Before prescribing lithium, order blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels, CBC, pregnancy test, thyroid function, and ECG for those over age 40 years.
Screen adults using the Mood Disorder Questionnaire and obtain collateral information from significant others if possible.
For patients aged 5 to 17 years, screen using self-report as well as collateral information from at least one parent and, if available, teachers, childcare workers, or significant others.
Two screening tools that show promise for children/adolescents are the Parent General Behavioral Inventory-Short Form (P-GBI-SF 10) and/or the Parent Mood Disorder Questionnaire (P-MDQ).

Drug therapy () is essential for patients with bipolar disorder during acute episodes to reduce symptoms and improve functioning. First-line therapy is mood stabilizers such as lithium, valproate and lamotrigine. Antipsychotic agents (quetiapine, aripiprazole, asenapine, capiprazine, and lurasidone) may be effective but have significant adverse effects. A A

Drug treatment decisions, referred to or made in consultation with a psychiatrist, should be guided by illness severity, history and current symptoms, patient preference, presence of comorbid disorders, medication efficacy, and side effect profiles of medications. C
Follow evidence-based algorithms to guide drug treatment such as those from the Texas Implementation of Medication Algorithms Project.
Reduce relapses, suicidal risk, and subthreshold symptoms through maintenance treatment, including both pharmacology and psychosocial interventions. A
Refer to a psychiatrist in most cases for definitive diagnosis and treatment.
Follow evidence-based algorithms to guide drug treatment such as those from the Texas Implementation of Medication Algorithms Project. Key recommendations are shown in .

Lithium is the oldest and best researched treatment for bipolar disorder and is used to treat acute mania and depression and for maintenance to prevent relapse. Studies have shown that it decreases relapse (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50-0.84). However, a systematic review of 12 studies with 2578 participants found no significant effect on death by suicide (0.2% vs 0.4%) or on suicidal behavior or suicide attempts. This was also the result of a VA randomized trial with 519 participants who had lithium added to their medical regimen for major depression or bipolar disorder.
An equation has been developed to predict the daily lithium dose. It has been prospectively validated and found to be accurate.
Other effective mood stabilizers include valproate and lamatrigine.
Aripiprazole may reduce mood symptoms in people at high risk of developing bipolar disorder.
A meta-analysis found evidence to support using a combination of lithium, valproate, or carbamazepine and an atypical antipsychotic as a first line of treatment for severe mania.

A meta-analysis concluded that antipsychotic agents plus mood stabilizers are superior to either group of medications alone in the treatment of acute mania. This review found no evidence of a superiority of second-generation antipsychotics over first-generation antipsychotics.

A randomized trial in 224 older (age 60+) inpatients and outpatients with acute mania compared lithium carbonate with divalproex. There was little difference between groups: those receiving lithium had more tremor and a slightly faster improvement, but at 9 weeks the response rate was 79% for lithium and 73% for divalproex. Only about 15% of patients in each group needed adjunctive risperidone.

A Cochrane review concluded that the response rate for adults with acute mania is better with valproate than placebo (45% vs 29%, NNT = 7) based on 4 studies with 869 participants. They found no convincing evidence that valproate differed from lithium in effectiveness for acute mania. Limited evidence suggests a similar effect for valproate compared with olanzapine. Evidence for effectiveness in children was lacking, though. There was no evidence that valproate and lithium differed on tolerability, although this evidence was of very low quality.
Like lithium, tamoxifen also inhibits protein kinase C and has been studied in 5 small randomized trials with a total of 186 patients. It was more effective than placebo for treatment of mania.

In 380 patients with acute agitation, a Phase 3 trial found that both 120 mcg and 180 mcg of sublingual dexmedetomidine significantly improved the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale-Excited Component score by 10 and 9 points compared to 5 points for placebo. A change of 3 to 4 points in the 30 points would generally be considered clinically meaningful. Adverse events included somnolence (21.4% to 20.6% vs 4.8%); dry mouth (4.8% to 7.1% vs 0.8%), hypotension (6.3% to 4.8% vs 0%), and dizziness (5.6% vs 0.8%). The drug is currently available as an injectable but has not yet been FDA approved for sublingual use.
A systematic review found 3 RCTs of gabapentin for acute treatment of bipolar disorder and provides some evidence that it was more effective than placebo for anxiety.
In 142 patients with bipolar II depression, a randomized trial found no difference in mood switch risk or treatment response between lithium, sertraline, or both.

For acute bipolar depression, quetiapine is most efficacious in response in short-term and relapse prevention profile for bipolar depression. Olanzapine (in combination with fluoxetine and to a lesser extent as monotherapy) and lurasidone are also effective with supporting evidence.

Lamotrigine has evidence for acute efficacy for bipolar depression both as a monotherapy and in combination with lithium and quetiapine, additionally it also supports relapse prevention (both recurrence of depression and mania).

In a systemic review and network meta-analysis which included 101 RCTs covering over 20,000 patients, olanzapine plus fluoxetine, lamotrigine were more efficacious than placebo in adults with acute bipolar depression by reducing depressive symptoms, with SMD 0.41 (95% CI 0·19-0·64) and 0.16 (0·03-0·29), respectively.
Rapid cycling is characterized by 4 or more episodes meeting criteria for mania, hypomania, or major depression per year.

A systematic review identified 30 studies of 16 drug therapies. They concluded that there was benefit for treatment of depression with olanzapine (with or without fluoxetine), citalopram, and velafaxine. They found evidence of benefit for mania for quetiapine, olanzapine, and aripiprazole. The pooled effect size for benefit was greatest for antidepressants in persons with a depressive episode and for antipsychotics in persons with a manic episode. However, the overall quality and extent evidence was relatively poor.

Maintenance treatments include FDA-approved lithium, aripiprazole, lamotrigine, and olanzapine and non-FDA-approved valproate and carbamazepine. Combination treatment may be needed if monotherapy is not effective.

Recommended first-line therapy is a mood stabilizer such as lithium, valproate and lamotrigine. Antipsychotic agents such as quetiapine, aripiprazole, asenapine, capiprazine, and lurasidone are somewhat effective but have significant adverse effects.

For the maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder, a recent Cochrane review concluded that monotherapy with valproate was as effective as monotherapy with lithium in preventing relapse, and was associated with fewer adverse events. However, a combination of valproate and lithium was more effective than valproate alone (RR = 0.78 for relapse). A second review looked at the efficacy of valproate for acute mood episodes, and found that it was somewhat effective compared with placebo for the treatment of mania (RR = 0.62, 95% CI 0.51-0.77). A trial randomizing 224 elderly patients to lithium carbonate or divalproex found similar tolerability and efficacy, with a somewhat greater reduction in mania scores with lithium.

A Cochrane review identified 6 studies with 1638 patients comparing topiramate to placebo or lithium. Topiramate was no more effective than placebo as dmonotherapy or as add-on therapy, and it was less effective than litium.

Adding an antidepressant to a mood stabilizer does not increase the likelihood of remission in bipolar patients with a major depressive episode and a recent report from the International Society for Bipolar Disorders could not "make broad statements endorsing antidepressant use but acknowledged that individual bipolar patients may benefit from antidepressants."
To increase adherence, prescribe the most tolerable formulation, discuss easiest medication schedule, and inform patients about possible side effects.
No randomized controlled trials of tiagabine (an anticonvulsant medication) exist on its effect for either acute treatment or chronic maintenance of bipolar disorder.
Antiglucocorticoids such as mifepristone, ketoconazole, metapyrone, and DHEA have been studied in small trials, with some evidence of benefit. Further study is needed.

For patients wishing to stop smoking, extended maintenance therapy with varenicline 1.0 mg twice daily for a total of one year significantly increased the likelihood of relapase abstinence at 52 weeks (60% vs 19%, NNT = 2) and 72 weeks (30% vs 11%, NNT = 5).

Consider electroconvulsive therapy for the following: severe or treatment-resistant mania or depression, mixed episodes, suicidality, psychosis, severe mania in pregnancy, and catatonia. NICE guidelines recommend ECT only for prolonged or severe mania or severe depressive illness.

A randomized trial assigned 73 inpatients with bipolar disorder and treatment resistant depression to either ECT or algorithm-based drug therapy. Response rates were higher for ECT (74% vs 35%, NNT = 3) but remission rates did not differ (35% vs 30%).
Consider vagal nerve stimulation in highly treatment-refractory cases.
One small RCT found the addition of omega-3 fatty acids significantly decreased the recurrence of mood symptoms compared with placebo.
A clinical trial randomized 46 bipolar patients to bright light therapy at midday or a placebo dim red light, and found a beneficial effect on remission rates and depression scores.
Bright light therapy has been shown to be effective in a meta-analysis.
A small randomized, sham-controlled trial in 59 patients found a greater response to therapy with transcranial direct current stimulation than with sham therapy (NNT = 6).
Refer to occupational therapist for help with functional impairment if needed.

Patients should be referred for cognitive behavioral, family, or social rhythm therapy along with psychopharmacology to improve functioning, enhance early syndrome detection, reduce relapse rates, increase drug adherence, and reduce hospitalizations. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy is effective.
Suggest patient keep a prospective daily mood chart to help identify triggers, to identify early warning signs of depressive or manic episodes, and to determine effectiveness of medication.

Adolescents aged 12 to 18 years (85% female) diagnosed with bipolar spectrum disorder were recruited from a specialty outpatient psychiatric clinic. The 100 participants were randomized to Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) and followed up over a mean of 47 weeks. DBT was significantly more effective than standard of care psychotherapy at decreasing suicide attempts over 1 year (mean 0.2 vs 1.1 attempts during the study period, p = 0.02).

Among 141 consenting patients with bipolar disorder and a baseline adherence rate of 67% to 69% for maintenance depot anti-psychotic injections, a modest financial incentive ($22) for each depot injection increased the adherence rate to 85% over a 12 month period.

An RCT randomized 145 adolescents with bipolar disorder to either drug therapy plus intensive family-oriented psychotherapy or drug therapy and family education (control). There were no important differences between groups.

A Dutch trial compared a collaborative care model with mental health nurses serving as care managers with usual care in 138 bipolar patients. Patients in the collaborative care group had better outcomes, with fewer months with depressive symptoms, and lower severity of depressive symptoms, but with no effect on mania or treatment adherence.

A study randomized 305 persons with euthymic Type 1 or 2 bipolar disorder to skill-oriented, material-based cognitive behavioral therapy (SEKT, an intervention that provides structured CBT while integrating elements of interpersonal social rhythm therapy, and of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy). Supportive, patient-centered, emotion-focused therapy (FEST) is psychotherapy emphasizes emotion-focused, supportive, and nondirective therapy. Both were equally effective at preventing relapse but there was no care as usual group.
Psychological interventions may be beneficial as an early intervention for people at high risk of developing bipolar disorder.

In a randomized trial with 205 persons with bipolar disorder, a smartphone self-management intervention did not improve the primary outcome of time to relapse. Relapse and manic symptom severity was decreased for low-risk individuals (HR, 0.32; 95% CI .12 to .88) but not for those classified as high-risk. Depressive symptoms were also decreased.
Drug treatment is long-term and involves treatment of acute manic, mixed, or depressive episodes and maintenance treatment to prevent future episodes.
There is a high risk of relapse in patients who abruptly stop medication therapy.
Refer patient to a psychiatrist for confirmation of diagnosis and pharmacologic treatment.

Consider hospitalization when patient is in acute manic phase, is socially isolated, has impaired judgment, has not responded to outpatient treatment, has medical complications, has psychotic symptoms, and/or is at imminent risk of harming self or others.
Document rationale for treatment setting and discuss treatment plan with approved family or friends.
Patients with comorbid substance abuse that is complicating treatment of bipolar disorder should be referred to a dual diagnosis program for treatment of both bipolar disorder and substance abuse.

Second-generation antipsychotics except ziprasidone and aripiprazole are associated with significant weight gain and increased risk of diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and dyslipidemia. American Diabetes Association recommends monitoring weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, glucose, and lipids.
Aripiprazole and lamotrigine may be a good alternative treatment for patients with side effects on lithium.
Begin drug therapy and medication monitoring, closely monitor patient's safety, treat medical complications, and reassess safety of patient and others before discharging patient.
Provide a structured environment during acute mania.
Provide illness education to improve insight and begin psychotherapy.
Conduct a family meeting for illness education, to answer questions and to complete discharge planning.

Regular follow-up is critical to monitor adherence to medications and side effects or complications of medications, to assess changes in mood symptoms or behavior and risk of suicide, violence, and impaired judgment or insight. C
Educate patients and their families about bipolar disorder and the treatment, prognosis, and strategies to prevent relapse. C

Lifetime risk for suicide attempts is 25% to 50% and for completed suicides is 15% to 20%. Patients are 30 times more likely to attempt suicide during a depressed or mixed episode than during a manic or hypomanic episode. B Patients with bipolar disorder have a higher risk for suicide with an annual rate of suicide (0.9%) compared to the general population (0.014%).
Bipolar disorder is a relapsing and remitting, lifelong illness with a variable course.
Approximately 90% of patients with bipolar disorder have comorbid psychiatric diagnoses.

Patients with bipolar disorder fluctuate between distinct phases including depression, hypomania or mania, euthymia, and in some individuals a mixed phase of depression and (hypo)mania. 15 to 25 years is the usual age of onset. First presentation usually involves depressive symptoms, and in the disease course, the majority (75%) of symptomatic time involves depressive episodes or symptoms.

Rapid cycling (four or more mood episodes in a 12-month period) occurs in approximately 16% of patients and is weakly associated with bipolar II disorder, female sex, hypothyroidism, and poor response to lithium.
Untreated patients may have 10 or more total episodes of mania and depression during their lifetime.

Among patients with biolar disoder, they were symptomatic during about half of the weeks in a median of 12.8 years of follow-up. Depressive symptoms during 32% of weeks, mania or hypomania in 9% of weeks, or cycling/mixed symptoms during 6% of weeks.
More than 50% of patients with bipolar disorder are not adherent to treatment.

Bipolar disorder often causes significant problems in many areas of social and occupational functioning or quality of life, including interpersonal relationships, emotional functioning, and family life.
Episodes of depression and/or (hypo)mania typically reoccur throughout life.
Maintenance pharmacotherapy may substantially reduce the risk of relapse and suicide.

Lifetime risk for suicide attempts is 25% to 50% and for completed suicides is 15% to 20%. Patients are 30 times more likely to attempt suicide during a depressed or mixed episode than during a manic or hypomanic episode.
Among children and adolescents (average age 14.4 years), the prevalence of suicidal ideation is 50.4% and suicidal attempts is 25.5%.

Life expectancy of patients with bipolar disorder is reduced by about 12 to 14 years in people with bipolar disorder, and specifically with increase in and sooner cardiovascular mortality compared to the general population. Over 50% of patients with bipolar disorder are not adherent to treatment and they also have higher prevalence of metabolic syndrome, obesity, cigarette smoking, and type 2 diabetes which contribute to their morbidity and mortality.

Follow-up should occur weekly in treating acute episodes of mania until signs and symptoms have subsided; thereafter every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months, and every 3 to 6 months once the patient is stable.

After prescribing an atypical antipsychotic, check fasting blood glucose, serum cholesterol, triglycerides, waist circumference, BMI and an ECG every 3 to 6 months, depending on the needs of the patient. Consider ordering a hemoglobin A1c once a year.
Educate patients and their families about the symptoms, treatment, and prognosis of bipolar disorder during inpatient and outpatient treatment.
Discuss the importance of medication adherence, maintaining sobriety, stress management, and engaging in structured activities, especially regular sleep patterns.
Encourage patients to keep a prospective daily mood chart to identify early warning signs of relapse and discuss how to manage early warning signs.
Encourage patients to follow through with referrals for psychosocial interventions, including therapists, case management, and support groups.
The diagnosis of bipolar disorder in older adults is more likely to be associated with a neurological or medical condition and less likely to be associated with a family history of bipolar disorder.
Older patients will usually be more sensitive to the side effects, including cognitive impairment, extrapyramidal symptoms, and an increase in falls.
There is a high risk for symptom relapse or exacerbation during the postpartum period. A systematic review found an overall postpartum relapase risk of 35% (95% CI 29%-41%).

However, some studies have found discontinuation of pharmacotherapy for bipolar disorder in pregnancy or postpartum is associated with a threefold higher risk of relapse compared with discontinuation of pharmacotherapy in nonperinatal women. People with untreated or undertreated bipolar disorder are at heightened risk of postpartum psychosis and suicidality.

The decision to continue medication during pregnancy, postpartum, and during lactation should balance the maternal and fetal risks vs. benefits. A systematic review recommended a slow taper if medication is discontinued, and to restart the medication immediately post-partum when the risk of relapse is high.

Continuation of pharmacotherapy for pregnant individuals with bipolar disorder is highly recommended by ACOG in the recent update on the 2023 clinical practice guideline No.4 and 5. For mood stabilizers, ACOG recommend against discontinuation except for valproate. Detailed second trimester ultrasound is recommended for pregnant patients who were taking lithium during the first trimester and lithium dosing monitored throughout pregnancy.

A systematic review of 20 good quality studies, and 29 overall, concluded that the use of lithium (especially in the first trimester) was associated with a significant increase in the risk of spontaneous abortion (NNH = 15, 95% CI 8 to 111) and any congenital abnormality (NNH = 33), especially cardiac abnormalities (NNH = 71).
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is an option for treatment with less fetal risk.
Obtain collateral information from a parent and if possible a teacher, child care provider, or significant other regarding child's longitudinal history of symptoms and functioning.
Children often have mixed mania, rapid cycling, and psychosis.
ADHD and conduct disorders are a common comorbidity that is unique to children and adolescents.
Mania is often manifested as irritability, hyperactivity, or temper tantrums rather than elation in children. The presentation of manic symptoms in adolescents is similar to that in adults.

An RCT randomized children with bipolar disorder to lithium (n = 53) or placebo (n = 28) for 8 weeks. Treatment was effective, with a greater likelihood of an Overall Clinical Global Impression-Improvement score of much or very much improved in the lithium group (47% vs 21%, p = 0.03, NNT = 4). There was non weight gain and the medication was well tolerated by the children in this study.

list.listitem: A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased activity or energy, lasting at least one week and present most of the day, nearly every day A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased activity or energy

During the period of mood disturbance and increased energy or activity, three (or more) of the following symptoms (four if the mood is only irritable) are present to a significant degree and represent a noticeable change from usual behavior:1. Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity. 2. Decreased need for sleep (eg, feels rested after only three hours of sleep). 3. More talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking. 4. Flight of ideas or subjective experience that thoughts are racing. 5. Distractibility (ie, attention too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli), as reported or observed. 6. Increase in goal-directed activity (either socially, at work or school, or sexually) or psychomotor agitation (ie, purposeless non-goal-directed activity). 7. Excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences (eg, engaging in unrestrained buying sprees, sexual indiscretions, or foolish business investments).

The mood disturbance is sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or to necessitate hospitalization to prevent harm to self or others, or there are psychotic features.

The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (eg, a drug of abuse, a medication, other treatment) or to another medical condition. NOTE: A full manic episode that emerges during antidepressant treatment (eg, medication, electroconvulsive therapy) but persists at a fully syndromal level beyond the physiological effect of that treatment is sufficient evidence for a manic episode and, therefore, a bipolar I diagnosis.Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed.; DSM–5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013)

feature.caption: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria for hypomanic episode

tr.th: A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased activity or energy, lasting at least four consecutive days and present most of the day, nearly every day.

tr.td: During the period of mood disturbance and increased energy and activity, three (or more) of the following symptoms (four if the mood is only irritable) have persisted, represent a noticeable change from usual behavior, and have been present to a significant degree: 1. Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity. 2. Decreased need for sleep (eg, feels rested after only three hours of sleep). 3. More talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking. 4. Flight of ideas or subjective experience that thoughts are racing. 5. Distractibility (ie, attention too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli), as reported or observed. 6. Increase in goal-directed activity (either socially, at work or school, or sexually) or psychomotor agitation. 7. Excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences (eg, engaging in unrestrained buying sprees, sexual indiscretions, or foolish business investments).
The episode is associated with an unequivocal change in functioning that is uncharacteristic of the individual when not symptomatic.
The disturbance in mood and the change in functioning are observable by others.

The episode is not severe enough to cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or to necessitate hospitalization. If there are psychotic features, the episode is, by definition, manic.

The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (eg, a drug of abuse, a medication, or other treatment). NOTE: A full hypomanic episode that emerges during antidepressant treatment (eg, medication, electroconvulsive therapy) but persists at a fully syndromal level beyond the physiological effect of that treatment is sufficient evidence for a hypomanic episode diagnosis. However, caution is indicated so that one or two symptoms (particularly increased irritability, edginess, or agitation following antidepressant use) are not taken as sufficient for a diagnosis of a hypomanic episode, nor necessarily indicative of a bipolar diathesis.
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed.; DSM–5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

feature.caption: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria for bipolar major depression

tr.th: NOTE: Criteria A through C represent a major depressive episode.

tr.td: A. Five (or more) of the following symptoms have been present during the same two-week period and represent a change from previous functioning; at least one of the symptoms is either (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure.

1. Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, as indicated by either subjective report (eg, feels sad, empty, hopeless) or observations made by others (eg, appears tearful). (NOTE: In children and adolescents can be irritable mood.)
2. Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all, or almost all, activities most of the day, nearly every day (as indicated by either subjective account or observation).

3. Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain (eg, a change of more than 5% of body weight in a month), or decrease or increase in appetite nearly every day. (NOTE: In children, consider failure to make expected weight gain.)
4. Insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day.
5. Psychomotor agitation or retardation nearly every day (observable by others, not merely subjective feelings of restlessness or being slowed down).
6. Fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day.
7. Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt (which may be delusional) nearly every day (not merely self-reproach or guilt about being sick).

8. Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness, nearly every day (either by their subjective account or as observed by others).9. Recurrent thoughts of death (not just fear of dying), recurrent suicidal ideation without a specific plan, or a suicide attempt or a specific plan for committing suicide.B. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.C. The episode is not attributable to the direct physiological effects of a substance or to another medical condition. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed.; DSM–5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013)

feature.caption: Maintenance Treatment Recommendations from the Texas Implementation of Medication Algorithms Project.
feature.feature_body:
Levels** Treatment Options
Most Recent Episode Hypomanic, Manic or Mixed
Level 1 Patients with frequent, recent, or severe mania: Lithium or valproate
Patients without frequent, recent, or severe mania: Lithium, valproate, or lamotrigine
Alternative: Olanzapine*
Level 2 Aripiprazole†
Level 3 Carbamazepine or clozapine*
Level 4 Quetiapine,† risperidone,† or ziprasidone†
Level 5 Typical antipsychotics,* oxcarbazepine,† ECT
Most Recent Episode Depression
Level 1 Patients with recent and/or severe history of mania: Lamotrigine combined with an antimanic agent
All other patients: Lamotrigine monotherapy
Level 2 Lithium
Level 3 Combination of an antimanic and antidepressant that has been effective in the past, including olanzapine-fluoxetine combination*
Level 4 Valproate, carbamazepine, aripiprazole,† clozapine,* olanzapine,* quetiapine,† risperidone,† ziprasidone*
Level 5 Typical antipsychotics,* oxcarbazepine,† ECT
*Safety issues warrant careful consideration of this option for potential long-term use. †Relatively limited information is currently available on this agent in long-term use. **Levels refer to a progression from Level 1 (most substantial evidence and least safety and tolerability concerns) to Level 5 (least evidence and greater safety and tolerability concerns). Data from Suppes T, Dennehy EB, Hirschfeld RM, et al.; Texas Consensus Conference Panel on Medication Treatment of Bipolar Disorder. The Texas implementation of medication algorithms: update to the algorithms for treatment of bipolar I disorder. J Clin Psychiatry 2005;66(7):870-886.
